connector: It’s Marilla. This is a hard chapter, and I’ll not pretend otherwise. Matthew was my brother, and the kindest man in Avonlea. Read it at whatever pace you need. If you have to stop and come back to it, that’s allowed. Anne and I got through it together. If it sits heavy with you, tell a grown-up you trust. There’s no weakness in that.

guide2.label: Marilla · before you open the book

rwm.label: Marilla · about Read like a Writer

transcripts.welcome: It’s Marilla. Today’s question is about grief, and how it moves. I’ll be plain, the way I always am. Matthew died, and this chapter is about the days after. Anne couldn’t cry at first. Then she could. There’s word work to do first, and that’s no bad thing. It steadies the hands. Then the chapter. Go gently with it.
transcripts.guide1: Word work first. It’s ordinary work, and I’ll tell you something about ordinary work. After Matthew, the cows still needed milking and the bread still needed baking, and I found the doing of it held me up. So take this the same way. One blank at a time, one word at a time. Do each one properly, and the next one will come.
transcripts.guide2: There’s a box here about being the one who carries it. Anne carried a great deal those first days. There were neighbors in and out, and there was me, and she kept herself steady for all of us. I didn’t see what it cost her until later. Read, and watch what she does in front of people, and what she saves for when she’s alone.
transcripts.rwm: This sentence is about me, and I’ll own it. I heard her, and I crept in. Notice the writer didn’t say I walked, or marched, the way I generally do. Crept is a careful word. It tells you somebody was trying very hard not to make things worse. When you write yours, choose that verb slowly. One right word can say a great deal.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. Take your time with these. One asks what happened that morning, one asks why Anne wanted to be alone, and one asks about laughing again. That last one surprised her. It surprised me too, a little. Answer each one plain and true, with something from the book to show it. Then rest a minute before the workshop. I’d recommend it.

a.raw: anne could not cry at first her grief was too deep for tears
a.fixed: Anne could not cry at first. Her grief was too deep for tears.
a.why: A capital on Anne, a period after first, a capital H to start the second sentence, and a period at the end. Could cry is helping verb + main verb.

b.raw: diana had offered to stay anne wanted to be alone
b.fixed: Diana had offered to stay. Anne wanted to be alone.
b.why: A capital on Diana, a period after stay, a capital on Anne to start the second sentence, and a period at the end. Had offered is helping verb + main verb; wanted needs no helper.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why the author mentions the white narcissus at that exact moment.
scholar.journal-q2: … and use her words about the dull ache to show what she is feeling.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say whether you agree with Mrs. Allan, and why.

fill1.h1: The topic is thrown under the sentence for everyone to look at. Which root means to throw?
fill1.why: ject means to throw: sub + ject = to throw under.

fill2.h1: Medicine is thrown into the arm. Which root means to throw?
fill2.why: ject means to throw: in + ject = to throw in.

fill3.h1: Copying spoken words across onto paper. Which root means to write?
fill3.why: scribe means to write: tran + scribe = to write across.

fill4.h1: Carving a name into stone is a kind of writing. Which root means to write?
fill4.why: scribe means to write: in + scribe = to write into.

g4w14ff1.h1: The winning came before Matthew died. Which helper puts something further back in the past?
g4w14ff1.why: had + won: had puts the winning before the other past event.

g4w14ff2.h1: This was going on for a while, back then, for one person. Which helper goes with having?
g4w14ff2.why: was + having: something going on in the past, for one person.

g4w14ff3.h1: Soon means it hasn’t happened yet. Which helper points ahead?
g4w14ff3.why: will + see: will points to the future.

g4w14ff4.h1: They means more than one person, and it reaches up to now. Which helper fits they?
g4w14ff4.why: have + faced: have goes with they.

s4w14ff1.h1: Run is one syllable, with one vowel and one consonant at the end. What happens to that last letter?

s4w14ff2.h1: Hope ends in a silent e, and the suffix starts with a vowel. What happens to the e?
s4w14ff2.why: Drop the e: hope + ing = hoping.

s4w14ff3.h1: Happy ends in y, with a consonant just before it. What does the y become?
s4w14ff3.why: y to i: happy + er = happier.

s4w14ff4.h1: Carry ends in y after a consonant, and the suffix is not -ing. What does the y become?
s4w14ff4.why: y to i: carry + ed = carried.

notes.wgrd: A hard moment shows who a character has become. Watch what she does, then ask what her younger self would have done.
vocab: A strong desire to achieve something important.
Comfort given to someone who is sad or disappointed.
Making something feel holy or set apart; deeply changing.
notes.wordParts: script and scribe mean “to write” (describe, manuscript). ject means “to throw” (reject, project).
notes.grammar: A helping verb comes before the main verb and sets the time: had won, will go. The main verb carries the meaning. Helpers can stack: had been waiting. Some verbs need no helper: went.
notes.spelling: Three suffix rules. Doubling: one syllable, one vowel, one consonant, so double it (stop, stopped). Drop the e when the suffix starts with a vowel (write, writing). Change y to i after a consonant, unless the suffix is -ing.
